title: Friendly to all
hook: Krishna: dear to me is one who hates no being, friendly and compassionate (Bhagavad Gita 12.13)
carry: a stranger at a bus stop

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Gita Govinda, and the flute calling through the trees. Your line was the flute. Today, Krishna speaks again, about whom he holds dear.

A battlefield, two armies facing each other, and in the space between them a chariot. The warrior Arjuna has lost his nerve, and his charioteer, Krishna, is talking him through it. That conversation is the Bhagavad Gita. By its twelfth chapter, Arjuna has seen a vision of Krishna's cosmic form, and now he asks a quieter question: who knows yoga better, those who worship Krishna in a form, or those who worship the formless? Krishna's answer winds toward a portrait of a person. And the portrait starts with one who hates no being.
screen: `A CHARIOT BETWEEN ARMIES.` → `ARJUNA ASKS A QUIET QUESTION.` → `A PORTRAIT OF A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Krishna says, in paraphrase: the one who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of mine and free from ego, the same in pain and pleasure, and forgiving, that devotee is dear to me. Notice where it starts. Not with prayer or sacrifice: with hating no one. The word for friendly, in Sanskrit, is maitra. Not friends with all, as if everyone becomes your best friend. Friendly: a basic warmth toward every being, the default setting of the heart. Right beside it stands compassion, karuna, which feels for those who suffer. The same verse joins friendliness to letting go of possessiveness and ego. Some readers hear a link there: unfriendliness can grow out of mine. My seat, my way, my turn. When the grip on mine loosens, there's more room to be friendly. And then, dear to God. Earlier in the Gita, Krishna speaks of devotion as offering. Here he says who is dear to him: the person whose love has spilled outward into how they treat every creature. Devotion to God, in this verse, shows up as friendliness to everyone else. A stranger at a bus stop becomes part of the practice.
screen: `THE VERSE: HATING NO BEING.` · `MAITRA: FRIENDLY.` · `FREE FROM MINE.` · `DEAR TO GOD.` · then, large: `FRIENDLY TO ALL.`

segments.voice: Picture a stranger you saw recently, someone in line, a driver, a person walking a dog, whose name and story you don't know. Let yourself be friendly toward them, not loving, not attached, just warm, the way you'd nod at a neighbor, and picture the nod you'd give if you passed them again tomorrow. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.
Maitra. The Sanskrit word for a basic warmth toward every being, the devotee's friendliness that Krishna calls dear to him. Today's word.
Your line: a stranger at a bus stop. In this verse, warmth toward every being is part of devotion. Day eight hundred forty-four, done.

howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and its twelfth chapter, on devotion, is sometimes recited on its own.

chat.says: Krishna says the devotee is friendly to all. Does that mean being best friends with everyone?
options: No, it means basic warmth toward every being, starting with hating no one.
Yes, the verse asks you to grow close to every single person.
No, it means being kind only to fellow devotees of Krishna.
chat.meaning: Maitra means friendly, not friends with all: a basic warmth toward every being, in a verse that starts with hating no one.
